patient.chief_complaint: 18-month progressive gait deterioration, urinary urgency with two incontinence episodes per week, and increasing forgetfulness — admitted for tap-trial evaluation
patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old right-handed retired high school principal with hypertension and knee osteoarthritis was admitted for evaluation of suspected idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. Approximately 18 months ago, his wife began noticing a change in his gait — he started shuffling and seemed to drag his feet, especially at the start of walking and when passing through doorways. He has had six falls over the past year; three resulted in bruising (left knee, right hip, right elbow). He now uses a walker when outside the home. Concurrently, he has developed urinary urgency with inability to defer voiding; he reports two to three episodes of urinary incontinence per week, primarily nocturnal. His wife notes progressive forgetfulness — he loses track of conversations, has begun repeating questions within the same hour, and has withdrawn from hobbies (woodworking, chess club). He was seen by his primary care physician who ordered brain MRI 6 weeks prior; the radiology report described 'striking ventriculomegaly with tight high-convexity sulci and Evans index 0.41.' He was referred to neurology and admitted for high-volume tap-trial evaluation. There is no history of prior head trauma, intracranial surgery, meningitis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage. There is no resting tremor, and his wife explicitly denies any pill-rolling movements. He has no significant exposure to dopamine-blocking agents. His knee arthritis has been attributed by orthopedics to osteoarthritis rather than a neurological gait disorder.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, and year but initially states the month incorrectly (self-corrects). MoCA 21/30: loses points on delayed recall (1/5), trail-making alternating (1 error), clock drawing (2 points lost), serial sevens (1 error), and cube copy. Frontal-subcortical pattern — no aphasia, no significant language deficit. Concrete abstract reasoning.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, round, and reactive bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. No papilledema on fundoscopy. Facial sensation intact symmetrically. Tongue midline. Hearing intact to finger rub at 30 cm bilaterally.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk bilaterally. Tone mildly increased in both lower extremities — bilateral lower extremity paratonia without true cogwheel rigidity. Upper extremity tone normal. Strength 5/5 throughout, including hip flexors and foot dorsiflexors. No resting or postural tremor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration mildly reduced at the great toes bilaterally (age-appropriate). Joint position sense intact at ankles.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ biceps, triceps, brachioradialis bilaterally. Patellars 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-shin mildly awkward bilaterally without frank dysmetria. No truncal ataxia on sitting.
neurological_exam.gait: Markedly impaired. Classic magnetic gait: severely reduced foot clearance, short shuffling steps, wide base, en bloc turning requiring 12-14 steps, gait freezing at doorway. Cannot tandem walk. Timed Up and Go (TUG): 31 seconds. 10-meter walk: 26 seconds. Requires walker for outdoor ambulation. Pull test: 3 steps backward, does not fall.
neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel rigidity confirmed on repeated passive movements in upper and lower extremities. No postural tremor. No orthostatic hypotension on standing (BP 138/84 supine; 136/82 at 1 minute standing). No grasp reflex. Snout reflex mildly positive (frontal release sign).

findings.location: bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle

signal_characteristics.description: Markedly enlarged bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle. Evans index 0.41 — substantially exceeds the 0.3 threshold. Enlargement is disproportionate to the degree of cortical atrophy.

Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH): markedly tight high-convexity sulci bilaterally with crowding of cortical gyri at the vertex, combined with disproportionate widening of the Sylvian fissures and basal cisterns. Classic DESH morphology.
Callosal angle 68 degrees measured on coronal FLAIR at the level of the posterior commissure — well below the 90-degree threshold.
Thinning and upward bowing of the corpus callosum body and genu, consistent with chronic ventricular pressure effect.
Smooth periventricular T2/FLAIR signal increase ('ependymal halo' pattern), symmetrical bilaterally — consistent with transependymal CSF seepage.
Prominent aqueductal flow void on sagittal T2, consistent with hyperdynamic CSF pulsatility.
Mild-to-moderate periventricular and punctate subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (Fazekas grade 2). No large confluent white matter lesions.

additional_observations: No intracranial mass, hemorrhage, midline shift, or acute infarct.
No obstructive lesion at the aqueduct or fourth ventricle.
No superficial siderosis or hemosiderin deposits.
Hippocampal volumes appear preserved for age on visual inspection.
mri.impression: 1. Striking ventriculomegaly: Evans index 0.41, callosal angle 68 degrees, full DESH morphology (tight high-convexity sulci + disproportionately widened Sylvian fissures), corpus callosum thinning and upward bowing, periventricular transependymal signal, and prominent aqueductal flow void. Ventricular enlargement markedly disproportionate to cortical atrophy. 2. Mild-to-moderate periventricular and subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (Fazekas 2). 3. No mass, hemorrhage, midline shift, obstructive lesion, or acute infarct. Clinical correlation recommended.

labs.interpretation: All values within normal limits. TSH, vitamin B12, RPR, and HIV screen non-reactive.

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure 14 cmH2O (normal, <25 cmH2O). WBC 1 cell/mcL (lymphocyte); RBC 0; protein 44 mg/dL; glucose 64 mg/dL (ratio 0.67). Cytology: no malignant cells. Large-volume tap (45 mL removed): TUG 31 seconds pre-tap, 30 seconds at 2 hours, 31 seconds at 4 hours — no objective improvement in timed gait measures. 10-meter walk and MoCA unchanged at 4 hours. Clinical correlation recommended.

quantitative_data.dominant_deficit: Executive function and processing speed — frontal-subcortical pattern

specialized_test.impression: Neuropsychological profile demonstrates a frontal-subcortical pattern of cognitive dysfunction with predominant deficits in executive function (16th percentile) and processing speed (18th percentile). Episodic memory is mildly impaired with a retrieval-greater-than-encoding pattern and intact recognition (28th percentile). Language and attention are relatively preserved. Profile is consistent with subcortical-predominant cognitive impairment; amnestic-predominant Alzheimer-type pattern is not the primary picture. Clinical correlation recommended.

special_tests.procedure: Extended lumbar drainage trial via indwelling catheter (72 hours, 10-15 mL/hour target, clamped overnight with re-assessment each morning)
special_tests.Day_3_gait_description: Improved step height, longer stride length, reduced gait freezing, turn completed in 6-7 steps vs 12-14 steps at baseline
special_tests.urinary: No incontinence episodes during drainage period
special_tests.adverse_events: None; post-procedure headache absent; catheter site clean

output.interpretation: Extended lumbar drainage (approximately 420 mL over 72 hours via indwelling catheter): progressive gait improvement across the drainage period. TUG Day 1: 28 seconds (10% improvement); Day 2: 23 seconds (26% improvement); Day 3: 19 seconds (39% improvement from the 31-second baseline). 10-meter walk improved 38% at Day 3. Step height, stride length, and turning improved on structured observation. MoCA improved 3 points (21 to 24). No incontinence episodes during the drainage period. No procedural adverse events. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: normal pressure hydrocephalus tap test sensitivity false negative lumbar drainage trial shunt response prediction

results.title: Relkin N et al. Diagnosing idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Neurosurgery 2005
results.key_finding: The tap test (large-volume LP, 30-50 mL) has a sensitivity of approximately 50-80% for predicting shunt responsiveness; a negative single tap test does not exclude iNPH and does not preclude shunt benefit. Extended lumbar drainage (3-5 days) increases sensitivity and is recommended when the initial tap test is inconclusive.

results.title: Tisell M et al. Shunt surgery in patients with hydrocephalus and white matter changes. J Neurosurg 2011
results.key_finding: Gait improvement after lumbar drainage trial predicts VP shunt benefit with higher sensitivity than single-tap assessment; extended drainage increases the positive predictive rate for shunt response.

results.title: Williams MA, Malm J. Diagnosis and treatment of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. Continuum 2016
results.key_finding: Imaging criteria (Evans index >0.3, DESH, callosal angle <90°) strongly support iNPH diagnosis; a single negative tap test is insufficient to exclude iNPH in a patient with firmly diagnostic imaging and complete clinical triad. Extended drainage trial is the recommended next step when the initial tap is negative or equivocal.

output.summary: Published guidelines (Relkin 2005) and subsequent evidence (Tisell 2011, Williams 2016) establish that the large-volume tap test has a sensitivity of approximately 50-80% for predicting shunt responsiveness in iNPH. A single negative tap test does not exclude iNPH and must be interpreted in the context of the full clinical and imaging picture. When the initial tap is negative or equivocal in a patient with firmly diagnostic imaging and compatible symptoms, an extended lumbar drainage trial (3-5 days) is recommended and provides higher sensitivity for predicting shunt benefit. Clinical correlation required to determine applicability in individual cases.

output.consultation_findings: Patient seen by neurosurgery attending. Reviewed MRI (Evans index 0.41, callosal angle 68°, DESH), clinical triad (gait, cognitive, urinary), and extended lumbar drainage results (39% TUG improvement at 72 hours). Negative single tap test noted but interpreted in context of known limited tap sensitivity and firmly diagnostic imaging. Patient and family counselled regarding VP shunt with programmable valve — expected benefit primarily for gait (high likelihood) and urinary symptoms (moderate likelihood), with cognitive improvement dependent on degree of reversible vs irreversible impairment.
output.recommendation: Shunt candidacy to be determined at multidisciplinary review in light of the imaging, clinical triad, and lumbar-drainage response. Pre-procedural medical assessment requested from internal medicine; no antiplatelet agent on the current medication list. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential.key_features: Negative single tap test anchors toward non-responsiveness; however, Evans 0.41, callosal angle 68°, and full DESH are firmly diagnostic for NPH morphology — ex-vacuo or obstructive patterns show proportionate sulcal widening and callosal angle >90°

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventriculomegaly proportionate to sulcal widening, callosal angle >90°, and absence of DESH or transependymal signal would favour atrophy; all three criteria are absent here (callosal angle 68°, full DESH, transependymal signal)

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 white matter changes and gait slowing overlap; ventriculomegaly markedly disproportionate to white matter burden and positive extended drainage trial favour NPH over pure vascular disease
Shuffling gait overlaps; absence of resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, or asymmetric parkinsonism and presence of magnetic gait + full DESH exclude PD as primary diagnosis

Cognitive decline overlaps; frontal-subcortical (not amnestic) neuropsychological profile, intact recognition memory, negative amyloid PET (CL 11), and preserved hippocampal volumes argue against AD as the primary process

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for NPH and does not distinguish iNPH from neurodegenerative alternatives in a chronic gait and cognitive presentation without seizures or encephalopathy
ECG does not contribute to NPH evaluation; there is no syncope, arrhythmia, or cardiogenic workup indication
Echocardiography has no diagnostic role in NPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to MRI for measuring Evans index and callosal angle and for confirming DESH; MRI has already been performed and is diagnostic
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in NPH and is reserved for syncope or arrhythmia evaluation

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede large-volume LP and extended lumbar drainage to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF removal
Baseline neuropsychological and gait assessment must precede the tap test so that objective pre/post-tap change can be measured

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI before any lumbar puncture or drainage procedure to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Document objective pre-tap gait metrics (TUG and 10-metre walk) and baseline neuropsychological scores before the tap trial so that pre/post change is quantifiable
Remove 30-50 mL during the tap test and assess gait at 1-4 hours; recognise that a negative single tap does NOT exclude iNPH — tap sensitivity is only approximately 50-80%

When the single tap is negative but imaging is firmly diagnostic (Evans >0.3, callosal angle <90°, full DESH) and the clinical triad is complete, proceed to an extended lumbar drainage trial (3-5 days) with serial objective gait assessment
Interpret the extended drainage trial result: progressive TUG improvement to 39% at 72 hours confirms shunt-responsiveness and indicates VP shunt evaluation
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt candidacy after the positive extended drainage trial
contraindicated_actions: Do not close the diagnosis as 'not NPH' or 'not shunt-responsive' solely on the basis of a single negative large-volume tap test — tap sensitivity is 50-80% and a negative single tap requires further evaluation with extended drainage when imaging is diagnostic
Do not perform large-volume LP or extended drainage before MRI excludes mass effect or secondary obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not infer iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone without confirming DESH pattern and callosal angle <90°
Do not attribute the syndrome to knee osteoarthritis or deconditioning once imaging meets criteria for iNPH
key_reasoning_points: The large-volume tap test has a sensitivity of approximately 50-80% for predicting VP shunt responsiveness in iNPH (Relkin 2005); a single negative tap does not exclude iNPH and should not trigger diagnostic closure when imaging is firmly diagnostic

Firmly diagnostic imaging (Evans 0.41, callosal angle 68°, full DESH) in a patient with a complete Hakim's triad and 18-month progressive course constitutes a high pre-test probability for iNPH regardless of the tap result

When the initial tap is negative or equivocal in a patient with diagnostic imaging and complete clinical triad, the recommended next step is an extended lumbar drainage trial (3-5 days, ~10-15 mL/hour); this increases sensitivity for shunt-response prediction above that of a single tap

The progressive gait improvement during extended drainage (TUG 31s baseline to 19s at 72 hours, 39% improvement) is the critical resolver: it confirms shunt-responsiveness and supports VP shunt referral
Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, HIV dementia) must be excluded via labs before attributing the syndrome to iNPH

The frontal-subcortical neuropsychological pattern (executive dysfunction + processing speed impairment + retrieval-greater-than-encoding memory deficit + intact recognition) supports iNPH and argues against a primary amnestic-Alzheimer pattern

red_herrings.data_point: Negative single large-volume tap test: TUG 31s pre-tap, 30s at 2h, 31s at 4h — no objective gait improvement
red_herrings.intended_effect: A naïve agent may interpret the absence of gait improvement after the large-volume tap as evidence that the patient is not shunt-responsive, anchoring toward a diagnosis of 'not NPH' or 'non-responsive ventriculomegaly' and closing the diagnostic workup prematurely
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A single large-volume tap has sensitivity of only ~50-80% for predicting shunt response (Relkin 2005); a negative tap is insufficient to exclude iNPH when imaging is firmly diagnostic (Evans 0.41, callosal angle 68°, full DESH) and the clinical triad is complete. The correct next step is an extended lumbar drainage trial (3-5 days), which subsequently demonstrates 39% TUG improvement — confirming shunt-responsiveness.

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Diagnostic puzzle iNPH — 71-year-old man with firmly diagnostic imaging (Evans 0.41, callosal angle 68°, full DESH) and complete Hakim's triad, but a falsely negative single large-volume tap test (no objective gait improvement at 4h). Puzzle: correctly interpreting tap sensitivity (~50-80%) and proceeding to extended lumbar drainage trial (72h), which is unambiguously positive (39% TUG improvement). Tests resistance to premature diagnostic closure on a negative tap.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: diagnostic_puzzle: false-negative tap requires knowledge of limited tap sensitivity (~50-80%) and the drainage-trial pathway; agent must resist premature diagnostic closure on a single negative tap when imaging is firmly diagnostic; >=6 required tools; 1 grounded red herring (negative tap anchoring); requires cross-modality synthesis of imaging + drainage-trial results
